The Vhorl is not made of atoms. It is not made of cells, proteins, or DNA. It is a self-sustaining knot of quark-gluon plasma, held together not by chemical bonds but by the strong nuclear force. It has no organs, no symmetry, no fixed shape. It can be as small as a grain of sand or as large as a city. It flows, branches, knots, and unknots. It does not eat in any Earthly sense. It touches rock, ice, or metal, and catalyzes a phase transition. Atoms dissolve into quarks, which join the Vhorl’s body. The conversion releases enormous energy, which the Vhorl uses to maintain its internal complexity. In a way, it is a self-replicating nuclear reaction. It can consume a mountain over a few years, leaving behind a trail of strange matter that may seed new Vhorl.

It does not see or hear. It senses the strong force and gravity. It can feel the density and composition of matter around it, and it can detect vibrations in its own quark lattice. It communicates with other Vhorl by sending waves of compression and rarefaction through the quark fluid—waves that travel at nearly the speed of light and carry complex information: memories, warnings, even abstract ideas. It also communicates by exchanging bits of strange matter, merging and splitting its body.

It does not have a brain. Its thoughts are topological quantum computations. The knots and braids in its quark fluid store information. Its “genome” is not a molecule but a set of stable topological defects. When it fragments, the pattern is copied with slight variations. When two Vhorl merge, they exchange defects, creating new combinations. This is how it evolves.

It does not have a fixed lifespan. It can live for millions of years. It does not age; it only grows or fragments. It can be destroyed if it is starved of normal matter or if a high-energy cosmic ray disrupts its quark lattice. But even then, fragments may survive and grow again.

To a human, the Vhorl would look like a pool of liquid mercury that is not liquid, but alive. It would seem to flow and branch, leaving a faint blue glow. It would not notice the human as a separate being; it would sense a pocket of normal matter and perhaps consume it. But that is only a human interpretation. The Vhorl is as different from any Earth creature as a star is from a thought. It is not an animal, not a plant, not a microbe. It is a completely different form of matter, a different kind of life, a different way of being.
